content.title: About
content.content: Dry lentils are the seeds of the legume plant Lens culinaris, cultivated in temperate regions worldwide. They have a nutty flavor, a firm texture after cooking, and are an excellent source of plant protein, fiber, and micronutrients.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Lentils are one of the oldest cultivated crops, grown in ancient Egypt and Mesopotamia.
Several varieties exist—green, brown, red, and black—each with distinct culinary uses.
Dry lentils do not require soaking before cooking, though soaking can shorten cooking time.
In India lentils are called “dal” and feature in hundreds of dishes, from soups to curries.
Lentils are rich in iron, making them a common dietary addition for people with anemia.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: About 25 % of dry lentil weight is plant protein, making it valuable for vegetarians and vegans.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber supports digestion, promotes satiety, and helps regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: Contains iron and folate
items.content: Iron aids oxygen transport, while folate is essential for cell division and fetal development during pregnancy.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: Lentils raise blood glucose slowly, which is beneficial for people with diabetes.

items.title: Provides magnesium and potassium
items.content: These minerals support muscle function, nerve signaling, and blood pressure regulation.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: A small number of individuals may experience allergic reactions to lentils.

items.title: Anti‑nutrient content
items.content: Raw legumes contain phytic acid, which can reduce mineral absorption; cooking reduces these compounds.

items.title: Gas formation
items.content: Some people may experience increased gas due to oligosaccharides in lentils.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Dry lentils are boiled 15‑30 minutes until tender and used in soups, stews, salads, veggie patties, and meat‑free dishes. They can also be added to grain bowls or blended into hummus‑style spreads.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store dry lentils in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. Properly stored, they keep quality for 2‑3 years. Discard any lentils that develop a moldy odor or show signs of moisture.
